evidence.title: Court suspends Thailand’s PM Prayuth pending term limit review
evidence.claim: Thailand’s Constitutional Court suspended Prayuth Chan-ocha from official duties while it reviewed whether the eight-year term limit had expired, leaving Prawit Wongsuwan as caretaker leader.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters wire reporting syndicated by Euronews; directly describes the legal constraint on Prayut’s authority.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within the 2022 ruler-period; it shows Prayut was not continuously exercising full PM authority after 2022-08-24.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attribution is to Prayut’s office and suspension status, not to nuclear policy.
contrary_evidence: This constrains authority but does not itself prove any nuclear-risk action or inaction.

reasons.reason: This is authority-timeline context from the term-limit suspension, not direct evidence of political freedom or authoritarian rule.

evidence.title: Constitutional Court rules Prayut can stay on as PM
evidence.claim: The Constitutional Court ruled that Prayut could continue as prime minister and counted the eight-year term from April 6, 2017.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous report of the official ruling with the key date logic and vote split.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022; clarifies the legal basis for his continued office after suspension.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attribution concerns his continuing PM authority, not nuclear decision-making.
contrary_evidence: Opponents argued the term should have been counted from the 2014 coup, which would have ended his tenure earlier.

reasons.reason: The court ruling about continued office is a legal-status reference, not evidence of democratic openness by itself.

evidence.title: Thailand signed and ratified the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons at the United Nations
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.claim: Thailand signed and deposited its instrument of ratification for the TPNW on 2017-09-20 and was among the first three states to do so.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary Thai government record of Thailand’s treaty act and the treaty’s prohibitions.
evidence.period_fit: Baseline posture predating 2022; useful for inherited commitment and continuity.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is state-level treaty action inherited by Prayut’s 2022 government rather than a unique 2022 decision.
contrary_evidence: The page is promotional and does not by itself prove 2022 operational restraint.

reasons.reason: Inherited TPNW ratification is state-level baseline, not a Prayut-specific 2022 existential-risk choice.

evidence.title: Permanent Secretary for Foreign Affairs reaffirmed Thailand’s commitment towards the achievement of a World Free of Nuclear Weapons at the First Meeting of States Parties to the TPNW
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.claim: At the June 2022 TPNW states-parties meeting in Vienna, Thailand said the treaty complements existing disarmament and nonproliferation mechanisms and took part in planning the treaty’s intersessional structure.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official Thai MFA statement with a precise 2022 date and explicit treaty-policy content.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand’s nuclear-disarmament posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is attributable to the Thai foreign-policy apparatus under Prayut’s government, not to a personal nuclear command decision.
contrary_evidence: The statement is multilateral and diplomatic; it does not show operational control over any nuclear capability.

evidence.title: Thailand hosted the 13th ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) Inter-Sessional Meeting on Non-Proliferation and Disarmament (ISM on NPD)
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.claim: Thailand hosted the April 2022 ARF nonproliferation meeting and emphasized the NPT pillars, Bangkok Treaty implementation, TPNW complementarity, peaceful nuclear uses with safety/security/safeguards, and cooperation on technological innovations and emerging technologies.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official MFA summary of a dated 2022 multilateral meeting with specific policy priorities.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to chapters 1B, 4B, and 8B as institutional context.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Thailand’s foreign-policy leadership under Prayut’s government, not to a personal nuclear command action.
contrary_evidence: This is agenda-setting and coordination, not proof of enhanced command-and-control or crisis restraint.

evidence.title: Country List : Office of Legal Affairs : IAEA
evidence.claim: Thailand has an IAEA safeguards agreement in force for its NPT obligations and an Additional Protocol in force; the country is also an IAEA member state.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary IAEA country fact sheet with treaty-status entries and dates.
evidence.period_fit: Stable treaty/oversight background relevant to 2022 and to Thailand’s ongoing civil-nuclear oversight.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is institutional state posture rather than a Prayut-only decision, but it constrains and channels any civil nuclear activity under his government.
contrary_evidence: Safeguards and an Additional Protocol are compliance mechanisms, not evidence of exceptional restraint by themselves.

reasons.reason: IAEA safeguards status is institutional context and should not be read as direct ruler conduct.

evidence.title: Thailand ratifies the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty
evidence.claim: Thailand deposited its CTBT ratification in 2018; the CTBTO noted Thai seismic and radionuclide monitoring stations and Thai tsunami-warning cooperation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary CTBTO press release on Thailand’s ratification and monitoring role.
evidence.period_fit: Pre-2022 baseline that remained operative in 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is national treaty/monitoring posture inherited by Prayut’s 2022 government rather than a unique 2022 command choice.
contrary_evidence: The release is about treaty adherence and monitoring infrastructure, not about any ruler-specific crisis decision.

evidence.title: สนธิสัญญาว่าด้วยการห้ามทดลองนิวเคลียร์โดยสมบูรณ์ (Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty: CTBT)
evidence.publisher: Office of Atoms for Peace, Thailand
evidence.claim: Thailand’s official nuclear-safety agency says the CTBT bans all nuclear explosions, Thailand signed in 1996 and ratified in 2018, and the country operates CTBT monitoring stations and a national data center.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Thai official source with explicit treaty history and the monitoring infrastructure located in Thailand.
evidence.period_fit: Stable background for 2022 civil monitoring and nuclear-test prohibition.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to state institutions under Prayut’s government, not to personal nuclear command authority.
contrary_evidence: The page describes civil monitoring and treaty compliance; it does not show a unique 2022 ruler decision.

evidence.title: Bangkok Treaty
evidence.claim: The SEANWFZ Treaty preserves Southeast Asia as a nuclear-weapon-free zone; Thailand is a ratified party, and states parties may not develop, acquire, station, test, use, or seek assistance for nuclear weapons.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent treaty reference with clear status, obligations, verification, and compliance discussion; not a live official registry.
evidence.period_fit: Long-standing regional baseline that shaped Thailand’s 2022 posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is primarily inherited regional law and institutional commitment rather than Prayut’s personal initiative.
contrary_evidence: NTI notes that the nuclear-weapon states still had not signed the Bangkok Treaty protocols, so the zone is not fully closed politically.

reasons.reason: SEANWFZ obligations are long-standing regional law; use only as inherited posture, not ruler action.

evidence.title: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW)
evidence.claim: The TPNW prohibits use, threat of use, possession, testing, transfer, stationing, and related assistance; Thailand is listed as a ratified party, and each party must keep existing IAEA safeguards.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent treaty reference with explicit status and compliance language; not an official registry, but detailed and stable.
evidence.period_fit: Useful baseline and interpretive framework for Thailand’s 2022 treaty posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The treaty position is state-level and inherited; it does not by itself show Prayut’s direct hand on existential-risk policy.
contrary_evidence: NTI notes that the treaty lacks its own verification regime and relies on existing IAEA safeguards.

evidence.title: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT)
evidence.publisher: United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs
evidence.claim: The NPT is the cornerstone of the global non-proliferation regime, aimed at preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear energy, and requiring IAEA safeguards for non-nuclear-weapon states.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN disarmament reference for the treaty’s role and safeguards architecture.
evidence.period_fit: Foundational background for Thailand’s 2022 treaty posture and regional nonproliferation commitments.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is global treaty structure, not a Prayut-specific action.
contrary_evidence: The page describes the regime framework, not Thailand-specific implementation quality.

evidence.title: Global nuclear arsenals are expected to grow as states continue to modernize–New SIPRI Yearbook out now
evidence.claim: At the start of 2022, nine states possessed nuclear weapons and the global total was estimated at 12,705 warheads; Thailand was not among the nuclear-armed states.
evidence.locator: press-release summary and world nuclear forces table
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative open-source arms-control data from SIPRI, published contemporaneously in 2022.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to the 2022 inherited global nuclear environment and Thailand’s limited exposure.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is structural context: Thailand’s leader did not inherit or control a nuclear arsenal.
contrary_evidence: The source is global context only; it does not attribute any personal restraint to Prayut.

reasons.reason: Global arsenal totals are structural context only and do not show Prayut-attributed restraint or risk management.

evidence.title: Radiation Safety Management Regulation of Thai Research Reactor-1/Modification 1 for Reactor Health Physicist Implementation
evidence.publisher: International Atomic Energy Agency conference platform
evidence.claim: Thai Research Reactor-1/Modification 1 was used for radioisotope production, nuclear technology research and education, and Thailand’s safety procedures required health-physics oversight and radiation-control checks.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: IAEA conference abstract from a Thai nuclear-institution speaker; specific but narrower than a full inspection report.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and useful for showing Thailand’s civil-nuclear, safety-governed exposure rather than a weapons posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional civil-nuclear management, not a Prayut personal command decision.
contrary_evidence: A research reactor is not a nuclear weapon capability; this is safety context, not existential-risk leadership proof.

evidence.title: MFA weekly briefing on Ukraine, 3 March 2022
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.claim: Thailand said it was following the Ukraine crisis with deep concern, supported peaceful settlement through dialogue, and voted in favor of the 2 March 2022 UN resolution because of the UN Charter, international law, sovereignty, and territorial integrity.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary Thai MFA record of Thailand's policy explanation and UN vote position in March 2022.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within the 2022 ruler-period and directly relevant to Thailand's international-security posture on Ukraine.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai foreign ministry under Prayut's government; not a private PM statement but an official government position.
contrary_evidence: Subsequent Thai abstentions show the line was not uniformly interventionist.

reasons.reason: This is an official foreign-ministry position on Ukraine, so it should be treated as state diplomacy under Prayut rather than personal PM conduct.

evidence.title: UN General Assembly adopts resolution on Ukraine, 2 March 2022
evidence.claim: The General Assembly demanded that Russia immediately cease its unlawful use of force against Ukraine, withdraw all military forces, and pursue a peaceful resolution through political dialogue, negotiations, mediation, and other peaceful means while protecting civilians.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN record of the resolution and its peace/humanitarian language.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and provides the legal-diplomatic frame for Thailand's supportive vote and later abstentions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is UN context rather than Prayut-specific conduct, but it anchors the decision Thailand was responding to.
contrary_evidence: The press record is not Thailand-specific and does not by itself establish Thai attribution.

evidence.title: MFA meeting with UNSG Special Envoy on Myanmar
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.claim: Thailand told the UN Secretary-General's Special Envoy on Myanmar that violence near the Thai-Myanmar border was causing civilians to flee into Thailand and that Thailand was ready to cooperate with UN and ASEAN mechanisms to find peaceful solutions and deliver humanitarian assistance.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary Thai MFA statement with clear date, named interlocutor, and peace/humanitarian commitments.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand's handling of Myanmar spillover.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai foreign policy apparatus under Prayut's government; Don Pramudwinai acted as deputy prime minister and foreign minister.
contrary_evidence: This is a diplomatic posture statement, not proof of successful conflict resolution.

reasons.reason: Myanmar spillover diplomacy is relevant, but the evidence is ministry-level posture rather than direct Prayut action.

evidence.title: Thailand scrambles fighters after Myanmar jet airspace breach
evidence.claim: After Thai fighters were scrambled in response to a Myanmar combat aircraft briefly entering Thai airspace, Prayut Chan-o-cha said the incident was 'not a big deal' and noted that a Myanmar defense attache had apologized.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters reporting with a direct Prayut quote and clear border-security context.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and relevant to a cross-border security episode involving a neighboring conflict.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Prayut's public handling of the border incident, though the underlying military response was carried out by Thai air force and defense officials.
contrary_evidence: Thailand still deployed fighters, so the episode was not purely verbal de-escalation.

evidence.title: Statement by H.E. Mr. Don Pramudwinai at the General Debate of the 77th Session of the United Nations General Assembly
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.claim: Thailand said that, as Myanmar's immediate neighbor, it had a vital interest in a quick return to peace and stability there, called on all parties to de-escalate, end violence, and engage in meaningful talks, and said it would continue to play an active and constructive role with ASEAN and the UN special envoy.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary Thai government speech at the UN with explicit statements on Myanmar, humanitarian assistance, and ASEAN process.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand's regional peace posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Don Pramudwinai as Thailand's deputy PM/foreign minister under Prayut; an official cabinet position rather than a personal PM statement.
contrary_evidence: The speech is aspirational and does not itself prove Myanmar policy success.

reasons.reason: UNGA speech by the foreign minister is institutional diplomacy, not a personal PM order or security decision.

evidence.title: Thai MFA summary of informal consultation on Myanmar, 23 Dec 2022
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.claim: Thailand hosted an informal consultation on Myanmar with Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, and Vietnam, describing it as open, constructive, and pragmatic and focused especially on humanitarian assistance and ways to support the five-point consensus.
evidence.locator: section 'การหารืออย่างไม่เป็นทางการเกี่ยวกับสถานการณ์ในเมียนมา (๒๒ ธ.ค. ๒๕๖๕)'
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary Thai-language MFA summary of a dated 2022 meeting with precise participants and purpose.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand's handling of the Myanmar crisis.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai foreign ministry under Prayut's government; Don Pramudwinai hosted the meeting.
contrary_evidence: Critics could see the meeting as breaching ASEAN norms, but the source itself frames it as pragmatic peace facilitation.

reasons.reason: The Myanmar consultation is a hosting action and should be framed as foreign-policy machinery, not personal conduct.

evidence.title: Myanmar shadow govt raises alarm after junta meets ASEAN members
evidence.claim: Thailand hosted junta ministers and other Southeast Asian officials for informal Myanmar talks aimed at a diplomatic path toward normalcy and the five-point peace process, but the meeting drew criticism from ASEAN actors who said it risked breaching the bloc's exclusion of junta representatives.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters reporting with both the host government's framing and the main contrary criticism.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand's regional conflict mediation posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thailand's foreign ministry and government hosting role, not to Prayut personally ordering a military operation.
contrary_evidence: Several ASEAN members skipped the meeting and critics said it was not helpful and could breach ASEAN policy on junta representation.

evidence.title: General Assembly Adopts Text to Suspend Russian Federation from Human Rights Council, Continuing Emergency Special Session on Humanitarian Crisis in Ukraine
evidence.claim: Thailand abstained on the HRC suspension resolution because it said suspending any UN member should not be taken lightly, supported an independent commission of inquiry, expressed concern over the humanitarian crisis, and renewed the call for political dialogue to end the dispute.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN meeting record capturing the Thai delegation's explanation of vote.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand's diplomatic posture on the Ukraine war.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thailand's UN delegation under Prayut's government; this is state diplomacy, not a personal PM statement.
contrary_evidence: Abstention is weaker than direct support for condemnation and can be read as hedging rather than clear alignment.

reasons.reason: This is UN-delegation explanation-of-vote material; keep it as government posture, not direct ruler attribution.

evidence.title: Thai PBS report on Thailand abstaining on Ukraine annexation resolution
evidence.claim: Thailand abstained on the UN resolution condemning Russia's annexation of Ukrainian territory while the Thai foreign ministry said Thailand still upheld the UN Charter, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and opposition to the use of force.
evidence.locator: opening summary and numbered explanation in article body
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Thai-language independent reporting of the government's stated rationale, contemporaneous with the vote.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand's Ukraine policy stance.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai foreign ministry under Prayut's government; not an individual military order.
contrary_evidence: The abstention reduced the force of Thailand's public opposition to annexation compared with a yes vote.

evidence.title: Thailand abstains in UN vote against Russia over Ukraine war
evidence.claim: Thailand abstained when the UN General Assembly called on Russia to bear legal consequences and make reparations for injuries and damage caused by the war in Ukraine, even as several ASEAN states voted for the resolution.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous English-language report with the vote result and Thailand's position clearly stated.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand's stance on Russian aggression and accountability.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thailand's government and UN delegation under Prayut, not to direct military command.
contrary_evidence: Thailand's abstention once again avoided a stronger anti-aggression vote despite support from some ASEAN members.

reasons.reason: The abstention is a state position on Ukraine accountability, not evidence of a Prayut-led military or coercive choice.

evidence.title: General Assembly Adopts Text Recommending Creation of Register to Document Damages Caused by Russian Federation Aggression against Ukraine
evidence.claim: Thailand abstained on a resolution creating a register of damage from the war in Ukraine; the UN text said Russia must be held to account for violations of international law and the need for a reparations mechanism.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN meeting record with the vote and accountability framing; directly contemporaneous.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and relevant to Thailand's accountability posture on the Ukraine war.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thailand's government and UN delegation under Prayut's cabinet.
contrary_evidence: Thailand's abstention again fell short of a clear pro-accountability vote.

evidence.title: World Report 2023: Thailand
evidence.claim: The Prayut government continued to restrict freedom of expression and assembly in 2022, prosecuting human rights and democracy activists, community advocates, environmental defenders, and critics of the monarchy; HRW says at least 1,860 people had been prosecuted since mid-2020 and that the protest movement was disrupted by criminal prosecutions, crackdowns, and surveillance.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary annual country chapter by a major rights monitor summarizing 2022 with specific counts and attribution to the Prayut government.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers events of 2022 and the surrounding legal environment that shaped them.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha and his government; this is office-level responsibility for the protest crackdown and associated legal regime.
contrary_evidence: This is broad pattern evidence rather than a single command order, and it includes continuity from 2020-2021.

evidence.title: World Report 2023: Thailand
evidence.claim: HRW says torture and enforced disappearance remained longstanding problems in Thailand, most reported cases were unresolved, and hardly anyone had been punished; it also notes abuses in the southern border provinces and during military custody persisted into the 2022 record.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct annual country chapter with specific findings on torture, disappearances, and accountability failure.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 because it summarizes the year-end safety and accountability environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attribution is to the Prayut government’s failure to secure accountability and protections within state custody and security operations.
contrary_evidence: The same report notes that the torture/disappearance bill was passed in August 2022, so the record is mixed rather than purely negative.

evidence.title: World Report 2023: Thailand
evidence.claim: In the southern border provinces, armed conflict subsided in early 2022 partly because the Thai military and BRN reduced violence during Ramadan, but attacks increased again from August despite ongoing dialogue; HRW says the government failed to prosecute security forces responsible for torture, unlawful killings, and other abuses of ethnic Malay Muslims, and often settled cases with compensation rather than accountability.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct country chapter with a specific 2022 conflict and accountability assessment in the south.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers 2022 southern-border conditions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Prayut government because it maintained the relevant security and accountability regime; the violence itself is partly insurgent and therefore not wholly ruler-directed.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes dialogue and a Ramadan reduction in violence, so the record includes some de-escalatory steps.

evidence.title: World Report 2023: Thailand
evidence.claim: HRW says Thailand continued to treat asylum seekers as illegal migrants subject to arrest and deportation, refused UNHCR status determinations for several groups, and kept more than 50 Uighurs and several hundred Rohingya in indefinite immigration detention.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct annual country chapter with explicit refugee-treatment and detention findings.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 vulnerable-group treatment and detention policy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Prayut government’s border and immigration policy, not to a single security operation.
contrary_evidence: HRW also notes occasional temporary protection for some detainees, so the picture is not absolute but still coercive.

evidence.title: Human Rights Situation Report May 2022: At least 1,813 individuals in 1,074 cases prosecuted
evidence.claim: TLHR reported that, by the end of May 2022, at least 1,813 people in 1,074 cases had been prosecuted because of their expression and participation in demonstrations, including 280 minors, and that most charges involved Section 112 and emergency-decree cases.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local human-rights monitor with direct case-count documentation and date-specific reporting.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and highly specific to protest repression under Prayut.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thai authorities under Prayut because the prosecutions were carried out by state institutions during his tenure.
contrary_evidence: The report shows some court acquittals and non-indictment decisions under the emergency decree, so enforcement was not uniform.

evidence.title: Thailand: Free Detained Critics of Monarchy
evidence.claim: HRW said two Thai pro-democracy activists were on hunger strike in 2022 because of prolonged pretrial detention on lese-majeste charges and urged the government to drop politically motivated cases; the article also notes that Prayut had ordered authorities in 2020 to restore lese-majeste prosecutions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights monitoring with explicit attribution of the restored prosecution policy to Prayut.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and also useful as attributable continuity from prior policy into 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable at the policy level because the article ties the prosecutions to Prayut's 2020 order and the 2022 detentions flow from that regime.
contrary_evidence: This is protest/political-justice repression evidence rather than a physical-violence incident.

evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Thailand
evidence.claim: The State Department said the Thai government restricted peaceful assembly, continued charging protesters under the COVID-19 emergency decree, sedition, and lese-majeste laws, and reported that 515 demonstrations occurred between January and August 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary U.S. government human-rights report with explicit 2022 event counts and legal framing.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the 2022 ruler-period and the protest environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai government under Prayut because it concerns national police and prosecutorial practice during his tenure.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes a constitutional right to assemble and some general access to bail, so the environment was repressive but not total closure.

evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Thailand
evidence.claim: The State Department noted that the Thai government lifted the nationwide COVID-19-related emergency decree on October 1, 2022, ending the most obvious nationwide emergency tool even though critics said it had been used as a pretext to arrest anti-government protesters.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary U.S. government report summarizing a dated 2022 policy change and the surrounding criticism.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and materially relevant to emergency-power use.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai government under Prayut, though the report notes this was a nationwide policy shift rather than an individual order in the text.
contrary_evidence: The same report says the southern emergency decree and martial law remained in force, so this was only partial restraint.

evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Thailand
evidence.claim: The report says the deep-south emergency decree and martial law gave security forces broad detention and search powers, limited access to counsel and family, and effectively provided immunity from criminal, civil, and disciplinary liability for officials acting under its provisions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary U.S. government report describing the legal architecture of coercive control in the southern provinces.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 domestic safety and the inherited security regime.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Prayut government because it maintained the emergency and martial-law framework; however the regime predates him and is partly inherited.
contrary_evidence: The report does not prove misuse in every case and notes some steps to investigate and punish officials.

evidence.title: UN Human Rights Office welcomes Thailand’s enactment of the Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearances Act
evidence.publisher: United Nations Human Rights Office for South-East Asia
evidence.claim: OHCHR called Thailand’s new torture-and-enforced-disappearance law a critical milestone, said it creates criminal accountability and non-refoulement protections, and noted that Thailand still had 76 unresolved enforced-disappearance cases.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN human-rights office statement on a dated Thai legal enactment with explicit accountability and remedy language.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to remedy and accountability reform.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai state under Prayut's government because it concerns enactment of a national law during his tenure.
contrary_evidence: OHCHR also flags unresolved disappearances and treaty gaps, so the law is an important but incomplete remedy.

reasons.reason: This is a reform milestone; it should not be double-counted as proof that enforcement already improved.

evidence.title: Law against enforced disappearance, torture published in Royal Gazette, takes effect after 120 days
evidence.claim: The Nation reported that Thailand’s first act to outlaw torture and enforced disappearance was published in the Royal Gazette, that it was signed by the King and countersigned by Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha, and that the act criminalized torture and enforced disappearance by state officials.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous local reporting of a formal legal act with explicit mention of Prayut’s countersignature.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to office-level responsibility for the new law.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable at the prime-ministerial signature level, though the legislative initiative was institutional rather than personal.
contrary_evidence: The article is procedural and does not show actual enforcement outcomes in 2022.

reasons.reason: Procedural coverage of the same anti-torture law should be treated as corroboration, not a separate event.

evidence.title: Thailand: Investigate Use of Excessive Force, Protect Right to Protest
evidence.claim: Fortify Rights said Thai police beat unarmed bystanders, kicked and punched protesters already in custody, and fired rubber bullets during the 18 November 2022 APEC protest crackdown, leaving at least 26 protesters arrested and at least 21 injured, with one activist reportedly permanently blind in one eye.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights investigation using photographs and videos, with specific allegations about police conduct and injuries.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to protest protection and use of force.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Royal Thai Police and, by extension, the Prayut government’s crowd-control chain of command; the article also notes that any orders or failures to prevent abuse could matter.
contrary_evidence: Police said protesters had assaulted officers, so the exact sequence and proportionality are contested.

reasons.reason: APEC crackdown coverage needs to be kept as one event family, not multiple independent incidents.

evidence.title: Thailand: Allow Newly Arrived Rohingya Access to Asylum
evidence.claim: HRW reported that Thai authorities detained 59 Rohingya who landed in Satun province, said the government treated Rohingya arriving at the border as illegal immigrants in indefinite immigration detention, and described a continuing pushback policy that could send boats onward rather than provide protection.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights reporting with specific numbers and explicit attribution to Thai state policy.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to vulnerable-group protection and detention policy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Prayut government because it concerns border and immigration policy implemented by Thai authorities.
contrary_evidence: Thailand did provide some food, water, and shelter to specific arrivals, but the core policy remained detention and pushback.

evidence.title: Thailand: Stop using force to crack down on APEC protests
evidence.claim: Amnesty International Thailand said the 18 November 2022 APEC protest crackdown caused at least nine injuries among protesters and four reporters and led to 25 arrests, criticizing police for using force instead of facilitating peaceful assembly.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous local human-rights reporting with concrete injury and arrest counts.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to protest repression.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thai crowd-control police under the Prayut government, with command responsibility potentially extending upward if orders or tolerance can be shown.
contrary_evidence: Police said they had injuries too, so the event involved clashes rather than one-sided force only.

reasons.reason: This duplicates the same APEC protest episode from another publisher family and should only corroborate the core event.

evidence.title: Thailand: Authorities must drop charges against child protesters
evidence.claim: Amnesty said Thai authorities had intensified a years-long crackdown on child protesters through intimidation, surveillance, and criminalization, with police and officials monitoring dozens of children and pressuring family members and school authorities to discourage protest participation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Amnesty report with direct allegations about monitoring, intimidation, and child-targeted criminalization.
